analysis.one_liner: Expands gun makers' and sellers' lawsuit immunity and immediately dismisses cases already in court.
analysis.headline: A House bill with 113 Republican cosponsors would broaden the gun industry's existing lawsuit immunity, dismiss every pending case covered by it, and block foreign governments from suing gun makers — but it has not moved since being referred to the Judiciary Committee in June 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act already shields gun and ammunition makers and dealers from most lawsuits over criminal misuse of their products. This bill rewrites that law to widen the shield: it would immediately dismiss every pending case that qualifies for immunity, expand which products, companies, and employees are protected, make it much harder for shooting victims to bring the few claims still allowed, let defendants move state-court cases into federal court, make defendants pay plaintiffs' costs when they win, and override state laws that try to hold the industry liable. It also bans any foreign government from suing gun makers or sellers.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, licensed dealers and importers, their owners and employees, and industry trade associations. They gain near-total protection from lawsuits over criminal misuse of guns — including the immediate dismissal of cases already filed against them, automatic access to federal court, fee awards when they prevail, and a ban on suits by foreign governments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the 2005 law's definitions so that immunity covers not just firearms and ammunition but also their component parts, magazines, optics, and other accessories, and extends 'seller' protections to the owners and employees of dealers, not just the businesses themselves [S2].
It orders courts to immediately dismiss any pending lawsuit that qualifies as a covered case on the day the bill is enacted — wiping out claims that victims have already filed [S2].

It lets defendants move state-court cases into federal court on a 'colorable assertion' that the suit is covered, requires victims to plead detailed facts up front to use any exception to immunity, gives defendants an immediate appeal whenever a court refuses to dismiss, and awards attorney's fees and court costs to defendants who successfully claim immunity [S2].

It prohibits any foreign state or government — including its agencies and instrumentalities — from suing gun manufacturers, sellers, or trade associations over criminal misuse of a firearm, and strips those governments of the usual exceptions to immunity [S2].
It preempts state and local laws that impose liability on gun manufacturers, sellers, or trade associations, in whole or in the way they allow such civil suits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People shot or otherwise harmed by criminal misuse of firearms, and their families, who would lose current or future lawsuits — including cases already in court. State and local governments would also lose their own laws as a tool against gun industry practices, and foreign governments (Mexico has a long-running suit against U.S. gun makers) would be barred outright.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shooting victims, their families, and state governments

drawbacks.text: Retroactive dismissal: every pending covered case would be thrown out on the enactment date, cutting off victims and families who already filed claims and have invested years in litigation [S2].

The redesign of exceptions makes them hard to use: a victim must plead detailed facts showing the seller was the proximate cause of the harm as a matter of law, negligent entrustment claims are limited to people the seller directly entrusted (a sale to a straw buyer who then hands the gun to a dangerous person would fall outside it), and if a criminal act caused a shooting it is deemed the 'sole proximate cause,' cutting off design-defect claims even where a defective product played a role [S2].

Procedure favors defendants: automatic removal to federal court, immediate interlocutory appeals of every refusal to dismiss, and fee-shifting against losing plaintiffs would raise the cost and risk of bringing any of the claims still allowed, deterring many victims from filing at all [S2].
The preemption section would override state and local laws that seek to hold the gun industry accountable through civil suits, taking policy choices away from states [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a large, one-sided gain to the gun industry — broader immunity, dismissal of existing cases, friendlier court procedure, and fee awards — while the cost falls on shooting victims and their families, whose remaining legal recourse would shrink sharply, and on states whose own liability laws would be overridden. Supporters would argue the industry should not be held responsible for criminals' acts; but the bill goes well beyond preserving that principle, reaching cases about product defects, straw purchases, and negligent sales already in the courts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 11, 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Derek Schmidt of Kansas introduced the bill with Rep. Glenn Grothman; both are Republicans [S1] [S2].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in its history [S4].
113 of the 223 House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat or independent cosponsor appears on the list [S3].
Because Congress is still in session and the bill sits in committee, it could still in principle move, but nothing has happened since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the gun industry: no new liability law has passed, and victims' pending cases remain alive only because the bill has stalled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and dealers, for now

for.name: Rep. Derek Schmidt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 113 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Democrat or independent did.

for.name: National Rifle Association and other gun industry groups
for.what_they_did: Long supported expanding the 2005 liability shield that this bill broadens; their support is the political base for the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 113 cosponsors are House Republicans (113 of 223); no Democrat or independent signed on, and the bill has not drawn opposition action in the record because it has not advanced.

industries.note: Immunity would expand to cover accessories, components, and magazines, pending cases would be dismissed outright, and foreign-government suits would be banned — directly answering lawsuits like Mexico's against U.S. gun makers. Their gain comes out of victims' ability to recover in court.

industries.industry: Gun dealers, importers, and their owners and employees
industries.note: The bill extends 'seller' immunity to individual owners and employees, not just licensed businesses, and adds removal to federal court and fee awards when they win. Narrowing the negligent-entrustment exception protects dealers who sell to straw buyers.
Trade associations are named as protected defendants in the immunity provisions and the foreign-government ban. Groups like the NSSF and NRA are the bill's natural constituency.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' bar and gun-violence victims as litigants
industries.note: Retroactive dismissal, heightened pleading, interlocutory appeals, and fee-shifting would sharply reduce gun-violence cases that can be brought or won. This is the group the bill's procedural machinery is aimed at.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly half of House Republicans signed on but zero Democratic support and no committee action since June 2026, the bill is likely to die quietly in the Judiciary Committee unless leadership elevates it. Even if it cleared the House, it would face an uphill path in the closely divided Senate. Gun-industry immunity bills have historically stalled at this stage; the most likely outcome is no further action before the Congress ends in January 2027.
